messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Rajesh

Rajesh had been an electrician for fifty-two years, a man who took pride in his steady hands and his knowledge of the city's wiring systems. At seventy-six, he still took jobs—smaller ones now, mostly residential rewiring and maintenance calls in the neighborhoods where he and his wife, Priya, had built their life. Three months ago, that life had fractured in an instant.

He had been leaving his truck on a side street near a commercial building on a Tuesday evening, tools locked in the bed, keys in his pocket. Two men approached from behind a parked car. One of them smelled of whiskey so strongly that Rajesh caught it before he heard their voices. They demanded his wallet, his watch—his father's watch, the one he had worn every day since 1985. When Rajesh hesitated, the taller man shoved him against the truck bed. The edge caught his ribs. The smell of alcohol grew thicker, more suffocating, mixed with the metallic taste of blood from where his teeth had cut the inside of his mouth. The second man's hand moved toward his jacket, and Rajesh had been certain—absolutely certain—that he was about to be shot. He had given them everything. They ran. He stood there, shaking, unable to move for what felt like hours but was probably minutes.

Since that night, Rajesh had not returned to electrical work. The thought of walking toward an unfamiliar building, of being in an alley or a dimly lit street, made his chest tight. But more than that, something had changed inside him—a fundamental shift in how he read the world. Strangers now registered as potential threats before he could think otherwise. A man standing too close in the grocery store, a teenager with his hands in his pockets walking past the house—these ordinary moments triggered a cascade of vigilance that left him exhausted. What frightened him most was the unpredictability, the way danger seemed to wear the face of anyone who approached him.

The nightmares began within the first week. He would wake at three or four in the morning, drenched in sweat, his heart racing as though he were still pressed against that truck. In these dreams, the outcome varied—sometimes the man did reach for a gun, sometimes Rajesh could not move his legs to run. The smell was always there. When he woke, gasping, the lingering sense of threat did not dissipate with consciousness. Instead, the dream's logic seemed to seep into his waking mind, leaving him convinced that the night itself was dangerous, that safety was something that only existed in daylight. He found it harder to feel secure after sunset, his body on high alert, ears attuned to every sound outside the bedroom window. Even inside the house, with Priya sleeping beside him, he would lie awake, monitoring, waiting.

Crowded places—the temple where he and Priya had worshipped for decades, the market where he used to linger and chat with vendors—had become intolerable. A few weeks after the mugging, he accompanied his wife to the temple for a festival. The sanctuary was full, bodies close together, the familiar warmth of community suddenly suffocating. When someone bumped against him in the crowd, his entire body tensed. A man's sudden movement near the altar—reaching up to light an oil lamp—sent Rajesh into a state of acute alarm. His mind flooded with the memory of the mugging, with the unpredictability of that moment when he could not anticipate what would happen next. He left the temple early, telling Priya he was unwell. He has not returned.

The smell of alcohol, which he encounters occasionally when someone passes him on the street or when a neighbor opens a bottle at a gathering, acts as a direct conduit back to that Tuesday evening. A whiff of whiskey at a restaurant, the faint aroma of beer from a delivery truck—and suddenly Rajesh is standing against that truck again, the threat immediate and overwhelming, his body flooding with the same terror, his mind convinced that danger is imminent. Priya has noticed that he no longer wants to go out in the evenings, that he declines invitations to dinners where alcohol might be served. What she does not fully understand is that for Rajesh, these are not mere preferences but desperate attempts to avoid the moments when his mind is pulled backward, when the distinction between then and now collapses entirely.

He came to the clinic because Priya insisted, because his sleep has become unsustainable, and because he is beginning to feel like a prisoner in his own home. He is afraid that this is simply who he is now—a man who cannot be safe, who cannot trust the world or the people in it. What he hopes for, though he barely dares to say it, is to feel like himself again, to walk into a room without his body braced for attack.
